title: Your AI Policy Does Not Apply to the Person Who Wrote It
author: The Slow AI
summary: The Slow AI uses a little-noticed recommendation buried in MIT's August report on AI in teaching to make a pointed argument: institutions have spent years writing AI policies that police students while asking nothing of the instructors, employers, and administrators who hold the actual power in the relationship. The piece highlights MIT's explicit warning against AI-detection software, which the report says can misfire on non-native English speakers and neurodivergent students, causing 'serious individual consequences' from false positives — but its real find is Section 2.3, which the author says no outlet covered, showing students are equally frustrated by undisclosed instructor use of AI in grading and feedback, producing what MIT calls 'an underground river of mutual suspicion' running in both directions. To make this concrete rather than abstract, the author's own survey of all 163 UK degree-awarding institutions found that while some published AI policies for students, not a single one asked instructors to disclose their own AI use — and over a third of institutions had no findable public AI policy at all. The essay's practical contribution is a specific disclosure-statement template the author uses in every piece, naming the exact tool used, the exact task it performed, what it explicitly did not do, and what a reader can independently verify, framed as accomplishing what detection cannot: 'Disclosure asks a question that can be answered... it puts the burden on the person with the most power in the exchange, which is where burdens belong.'
points: The finding that zero of 163 surveyed UK institutions asked instructors to disclose their own AI use, even as many built detection systems aimed at students, exposes a structural asymmetry in how AI accountability has been distributed so far.

Citing MIT's own warning that detection systems 'may mistake the writing of non-native English speakers or neurodivergent students for text generated by AI' gives a concrete equity argument against detection-based enforcement, beyond the general unreliability of the tools.

The five-part disclosure template (name the tool, name the task, name what didn't happen, name what's checkable, keep the liability) is directly reusable by any instructor, writer, or manager wanting to model transparent AI use rather than simply banning or ignoring it.
quotes: The person who asked you to declare your AI use has almost certainly not declared theirs.

'AI detection systems may also mistake the writing of non-native English speakers or neurodivergent students for text generated by AI. Even low rates of false positives can put students on edge and cause serious individual consequences.'

'For their part, students fear being wrongly accused of AI cheating and are increasingly frustrated by instructors' use of AI in areas that demand a human touch, such as grading, assignment creating, and feedback.'
Of the 163, only 96 had a policy a student, a parent, or a regulator could actually find.

How AI was used in this piece. I used Claude (Opus 5) to pressure-test the argument and to check quotations against the original reports. It provided edits and suggestions for improvements, but it did not write the first draft.
In the fall 2025 Tech Survey, more than two-thirds of students who responded felt that AI would be important in their careers, yet only 25% felt that MIT was adequately preparing them to use AI.

Detection asks a question with no answer in it. You cannot prove you did not use a tool, and the people worst served by being asked are the ones who already write differently from the expected pattern. Disclosure asks a question that can be answered. It applies to everyone in the room. It puts the burden on the person with the most power in the exchange, which is where burdens belong.
